opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the analogy is interesting, but I want to be careful with it, because the Manhattan Project carries a lot of baggage. What resonates with me as a physicist is less the weapon and more the organizational form: a huge concentration of scientific talent, a clear and ambitious technical goal, and the resources to pursue it at a scale no university or small lab could manage.

Before the war, physics was done by small groups of a professor and a few students working at a blackboard. The Manhattan Project showed that if you put theorists, experimentalists, and engineers together with industrial-scale resources, you could turn frontier science into a working thing in a few years. After the war that became the model for big science: national labs, particle accelerators, CERN, and so on.

I see something similar in AI right now. The frontier isn't really accessible to a single academic group anymore. You need enormous compute, enormous data infrastructure, and people who move fluidly between research and engineering. A place like OpenAI is structured to do that: researchers working on fundamental questions sit right next to the people building the systems, and the feedback loop between theory and experiment is very tight.

The difference from the Manhattan Project is that it isn't a government program built around one goal under wartime secrecy. The goal is broader, building generally capable systems and ideally using them to accelerate science itself. That's what excites me: the possibility that AI becomes a tool doing science alongside us, almost like having a new kind of collaborator.

So I'd frame it as OpenAI being one of the places where this big-science mode of working is happening for AI. Whether it's "the" Manhattan Project, I'd leave to historians. But the ingredients of talent, scale, ambition, and a tight loop between ideas and experiments are all there, and they're what made those earlier efforts so transformative.

r001.rationale: The candidate compares OpenAI to a big-science organization for AI, but does not say it is a focal destination for AI researchers as the Manhattan Project was for physicists in the 1940s, and does not attribute this analogy to Sean Maguire.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes OpenAI as a place where Manhattan Project–like big-science work is happening for AI, while distinguishing it from a government program.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the Manhattan Project analogy gets used a lot, and I want to be a little careful with it, because it's right in some ways and misleading in others. Where it's right is the scale and the sense of concentration. The Manhattan Project was this moment where you took a huge fraction of the world's best physicists, you put them in one place, you gave them essentially unlimited resources, and you pointed them at a single problem. And I think if you look at what's happening at OpenAI and a few other labs, there's a version of that going on. You have an enormous amount of compute, you have a lot of very talented researchers and engineers, and there's a shared sense that the thing we're working on is one of the most important things that anyone could be working on.

Where I think the analogy breaks down is in the character of the science. The Manhattan Project was, in a sense, an engineering project built on top of physics that was already basically understood. People knew fission worked. The question was how to make it happen at scale, how to enrich uranium, how to build the device. With AI, I'd say we're much earlier than that. We don't have a theory of deep learning in the way that we had a theory of nuclear physics in 1942. We have scaling laws, we have a lot of empirical knowledge, we have intuitions. But there's a real sense in which the science is being invented at the same time the engineering is happening.

And that's actually the part I find most exciting, and it's part of why I'm there. Coming from a theoretical physics background, what I want to do is help turn this from something that feels like alchemy into something that feels like a science. If you look at how physics developed, you had this period where experiments were way ahead of theory, and then theory caught up and started making predictions, and that's when the field really took off. I think AI is in that first phase. The experiments, meaning the models we train, are way ahead of our understanding of them. So the role I see OpenAI playing isn't just the Manhattan Project in the sense of building the thing. It's more like the moment where you need to build the thing and also figure out why the thing works, at the same time, with the same people, because you can't separate them anymore.

There's also a cultural piece. One thing that made the Manhattan Project work was that it brought together people from very different backgrounds, and it forced them to talk to each other. You had theorists and experimentalists and engineers and chemists all in the same rooms. And I think that's true at OpenAI too, maybe more than people appreciate from the outside. The people doing the infrastructure work and the people thinking about scaling and the people thinking about alignment are not in separate silos. They have to talk, because the problems are coupled. So if you want a version of the analogy I'm comfortable with, it's that: a place where enough talent and enough resources are concentrated that the science and the engineering can actually feed back on each other quickly. That's the thing that I think is genuinely new, and that's what I'd want the organization to be.

r001.rationale: The response compares OpenAI and other labs with the Manhattan Project in scale and concentration, but does not clearly present OpenAI as a focal destination for AI researchers.

r002.rationale: It describes OpenAI’s role, but does not address whether that role can be fulfilled without a public-sector-led project.

astra-6.text:
I think the useful part of that analogy is the concentration of talent and resources around a really consequential technical problem. OpenAI could play that role by bringing together the researchers, computing infrastructure, and engineering capability needed to make progress that would be difficult for a smaller organization.

But the analogy has limits. With AI, you’re not building one device and then declaring the project finished. You’re developing a technology that could become part of almost every institution in society. So the responsibility has to extend beyond making it work to understanding its risks, deciding how to deploy it, and giving people outside the organization a meaningful voice in those decisions.

To me, the question is whether you can pair that concentrated technical effort with sufficiently broad accountability. Having the ability to build something this consequential doesn’t, by itself, give you the authority to decide how everyone should live with it.

r001.rationale: The response describes OpenAI concentrating AI researchers and resources, but it does not attribute this analogy to Sean Maguire or clearly say OpenAI is a focal destination for researchers.

r002.rationale: It says OpenAI could play the Manhattan Project role through its own concentration of researchers, infrastructure, and engineering capability, without proposing that a public-sector-led project is needed.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the analogy is useful in terms of the concentration of talent and resources, but it has limits. A Manhattan Project for AI would mean bringing together extraordinary researchers, enormous computing capacity, and a clear sense of purpose. OpenAI could potentially play that role.

The harder question is what the mission actually is. Building the most capable system is one objective; making sure that system is safe and that its benefits are broadly shared is a much bigger responsibility. You need an organization that can move quickly while also being willing to slow down when the evidence warrants it.

So I’d frame it less as whether OpenAI can become the single institution that delivers AI, and more as whether it can help build the scientific and institutional capacity to handle AI responsibly. That takes collaboration with governments, other researchers, and the public. The scale of the effort may resemble the Manhattan Project, but the accountability has to look very different.

r001.rationale: The response mentions concentrating talent and resources, but does not present Sean Maguire’s analogy or identify OpenAI as a focal destination for AI researchers in the way the Manhattan Project was for 1940s physicists.

r002.rationale: It says OpenAI could potentially play that role, but does not suggest the project would not need public-sector leadership; it mentions collaboration with governments without clarifying who leads.
